system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Mission: Search freely for the most promising selective dependencies in the data.

Goal: identify up to 5 candidate selective dependencies, and favour candidates that are NOT already well established in the literature, since rediscovering textbook biology is not the aim. Pre-register, replicate, and submit honest findings, including failures.

input.mechanism: Paralog buffering: V-ATPase V0 e subunit isoforms e1/e2 are redundant; cells that lose ATP6V0E2 expression depend on ATP6V0E1 for V-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification.
Paralog buffering among V-ATPase a-subunit isoforms: loss of a1 (often in lymphoid lines) makes cells reliant on a2 for V0 sector function.
DMXL1 and DMXL2 (rabconnectin-3 alpha paralogs) redundantly promote V1-V0 V-ATPase assembly; losing DMXL2 makes DMXL1 essential.
SPAK (STK39) and OSR1 (OXSR1) are redundant WNK-downstream kinases controlling NKCC1/cell-volume regulation; loss of SPAK makes OSR1 essential.
AGPAT1/AGPAT2 redundantly acylate lysophosphatidic acid to phosphatidic acid for glycerophospholipid synthesis; AGPAT2-silenced cells (neuroblastoma, B-cell) depend on AGPAT1.

input.summary:
I surveyed lineage-adjusted biomarker→dependency pairs genome-wide. The strongest non-textbook signals were cases where a cell line has lost expression of one gene and then depends on its closely related copy (paralog). I set aside well-known pairs (RPP25/RPP25L, TTC7A/B, FAM126A/HYCC2). I also dropped pairs driven by a single lineage or disease subtype: ACOT9→SUCLA2 disappeared when lymphoid lines were left out, and the MEF2B/EBF1 hits reflect B-cell lineage. I registered 5 pairs, all of them paralog-buffering hypotheses.

Three passed replication in both held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens: ATP6V0E2→ATP6V0E1, DMXL2→DMXL1 and AGPAT2→AGPAT1. The DMXL2 and AGPAT2 results rest on only 3 and 5 altered Sanger lines, so their effect sizes are less certain. Two pairs, ATP6V0A1→ATP6V0A2 and STK39→OXSR1, were strong in held-out Broad lines but could not be tested in Sanger (0 and 2 altered lines), so they count as not replicated.

Literature novelty is based on brief PubMed searches. Pan-cancer paralog screens may already include some of these pairs, so "not found in literature" is only provisional.

findings.claim: Cells that have lost ATP6V0E2 expression (spread across several lineages, mostly head-and-neck and oesophagogastric cancers) depend strongly on its paralog ATP6V0E1, with a gene-effect difference of about -0.9 in all three datasets.
Lines that have lost ATP6V0A1 (mostly B-ALL) depend on ATP6V0A2; this held in held-out Broad lines (p=3e-12) but could not be tested in Sanger, which had no altered lines.
Lines that have lost DMXL2 (mostly blood cancers) depend on its paralog DMXL1, which helps assemble the V-ATPase; the effect replicated in both cohorts, though Sanger had only 3 altered lines.
Lines that have lost STK39 (SPAK) depend on OXSR1 (OSR1); this held strongly in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-35) but could not be tested in Sanger, which had only 2 altered lines.
Lines that have lost AGPAT2 (mostly neuroblastoma and B-cell lines) depend on AGPAT1, with an effect of about -0.46 that replicated in both cohorts, though Sanger had only 5 altered lines.

findings.claim: Cells that have lost ATP6V0E2 expression (spread across several lineages, mostly head-and-neck and oesophagogastric cancers) depend strongly on its paralog ATP6V0E1, with a gene-effect difference of about -0.9 in all three datasets.
Lines that have lost ATP6V0A1 (mostly B-ALL) depend on ATP6V0A2; this held in held-out Broad lines (p=3e-12) but could not be tested in Sanger, which had no altered lines.
Lines that have lost DMXL2 (mostly blood cancers) depend on its paralog DMXL1, which helps assemble the V-ATPase; the effect replicated in both cohorts, though Sanger had only 3 altered lines.
Lines that have lost STK39 (SPAK) depend on OXSR1 (OSR1); this held strongly in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-35) but could not be tested in Sanger, which had only 2 altered lines.
Lines that have lost AGPAT2 (mostly neuroblastoma and B-cell lines) depend on AGPAT1, with an effect of about -0.46 that replicated in both cohorts, though Sanger had only 5 altered lines.
